title: Archipelago Civilization History
planning_principle: The 24 regions are distinct civilizations that developed independently from local climate, resources, hazards and geography. Trade, migration, war, pilgrimage and imitation caused cultural borrowing, but no region is a simple reskin or colony of another. Borrowed ideas are always translated through local building methods and values.

eras.name: Age of First Hearths
eras.summary: Scattered communities developed independently around the archipelago: northern hall-builders, lake villages, forest clans, canal farmers, highland masons, mesa potters, wetland pile-settlers, reef navigators and tropical husbandry communities. Crystal Deep contains ruins that appear older than any surviving surface tradition.

eras.name: Age of Roads and Sails
eras.summary: Reliable coastal sailing, mountain passes, canals and maintained forest roads connected previously isolated cultures. This was the first sustained period of architectural borrowing. Crownlands civic planning, Stone Highlands masonry, Timberlands carpentry, Red Clay Basin brickwork and Sapphire Coast navigation spread widely but were adapted locally.

eras.name: Age of Crowns and Compacts
eras.summary: Larger states and regional leagues emerged. The Crownlands consolidated central political power, the High Kingdom unified mountain strongholds, Breadbasket canal communities formed a food compact, and Timberlands guilds formalized forest stewardship. Border wars were common but rarely erased local identities.

eras.name: Age of Exchange
eras.summary: The Grand Exchange grew from a neutral seasonal market into the archipelago's dominant commercial port. Trade became dense enough that specialized regions could depend on one another. Engineer's Reach and Artisan Coast rose during this era from mixed technical and craft communities while developing their own civic identities.

eras.name: Age of Gates
eras.summary: Portal engineering and long-distance transportation transformed the world. Ember Coast grew around dangerous Nether access, Transit Isles standardized interregional movement, and later Shrouded Isles settlements appeared after sustained End expeditions. These younger cultures are more visibly hybrid, but isolation and specialized environments quickly made them distinct.

eras.name: Present Concord
eras.summary: The archipelago is interconnected without being politically unified. Most regions accept the Transit Accords governing major routes and Grand Exchange commercial law for interregional trade, while local law, architecture and custom remain sovereign. Rivalries, old grievances and competing prestige projects still shape the world.

major_historical_events.name: The Three Bridges War
major_historical_events.summary: A struggle over mountain crossings and taxation ended after Stone Highlands bridge-builders forced both powers to recognize neutral access rights. Crownlands and High Kingdom architecture still display competitive bridge and gate monuments from the period.

major_historical_events.name: The Greenbank Dispute
major_historical_events.summary: Forest clearing, river diversion and downstream mills nearly caused a long regional conflict. The resulting Greenbank Compact established protected headwaters, managed forest belts and shared mill rights. It explains why the Timberlands retains old-growth reserves despite enormous demand for wood.

major_historical_events.name: The Drowning Years
major_historical_events.summary: A sequence of severe storms and shoreline changes destroyed older low coastal settlements. Refugees and engineers exchanged stilt, seawall and channel-control techniques. Each region remembers the disaster differently, creating three related but visibly distinct water-building traditions.

major_historical_events.name: The Freeport Crisis
major_historical_events.summary: Privateers, smugglers and merchant fleets fought over tariffs and safe passage. No side achieved control. Pirate Island became a tolerated independent freeport, while Sapphire Coast developed stronger sea gates and Grand Exchange created bonded customs harbors.

major_historical_events.name: The Ash Compact
major_historical_events.summary: Early portal industries repeatedly failed because ordinary surface construction could not survive heat and hostile conditions. Volcano masons and Engineer's Reach technicians helped formalize protected portal courts and compartmentalized industrial districts. Ember Coast later transformed these borrowed techniques into its own fortress-industrial culture.

major_historical_events.name: The Transit Accords
major_historical_events.summary: After repeated disputes over tolls, navigation markers and freight priority, the Transit Isles negotiated a common system of signs, route standards, emergency harbors and neutral passenger facilities. This is the closest thing the archipelago has to shared infrastructure law.

The Great Cold North.origin: One of the oldest surviving surface traditions. Northern hall-builders formed isolated kin settlements around protected valleys and winter harbors rather than a centralized kingdom.
The Great Cold North.identity: Communal memory, endurance, hospitality within the hall and suspicion of unnecessary urban density.
influences_received: High Kingdom stone craft in a few late prestige structures
Frost Marches market goods and frontier carpentry
influences_given: Great-hall traditions to Frost Marches
winter refuge customs to Shattered Ice Coast
The Great Cold North.relations: Friendly but culturally distant from Frost Marches; respected by Shattered Ice Coast sailors; largely indifferent to Crownlands politics.
The Great Cold North.trade: Exports ice, rare northern materials and expedition goods; imports grain, metal tools, finished cloth-like goods and brewing supplies.
The Great Cold North.historic_landmark: The First Hall, an enormous stone-plinth timber hall rebuilt repeatedly around an older megalithic core.
The Great Cold North.routes: Northern Beacon Route: Frost Marches -> Shattered Ice Coast -> Great Cold North.

Frost Marches.origin: Developed at the contact zone between northern hall communities, taiga settlements and merchants moving north from the central regions.
Frost Marches.identity: Practical frontier cooperation, defended markets, winter storage and a culture comfortable borrowing useful ideas without adopting foreign ceremony.
influences_given: cold-weather carpentry to Shattered Ice Coast
frontier fortification ideas to northern settlements
Frost Marches.relations: Acts as mediator between the far north and central regions; generally cordial with Timberlands and wary of Crownlands tax collectors.
Frost Marches.trade: Exports taiga products, cold-weather goods and northern transit services; imports grain, stone, metal and luxury goods.
Frost Marches.historic_landmark: The Covered Market, rebuilt after several winter fires and now the model for frontier civic halls.
Frost Marches.routes: North Road to the Great Cold North; Ice Road to Shattered Ice Coast; southern timber road toward Crownlands markets.

Shattered Ice Coast.origin: Independent maritime communities formed around protected coves where ship repair, wreck salvage and cold-water fishing were more reliable than inland farming.
Shattered Ice Coast.identity: Sea survival, salvage prestige, beacon keeping and strong local loyalty among otherwise competitive ports.
influences_received: High Kingdom monastic forms on remote cliffs
influences_given: storm harbor design to northern Transit stations
wreck-timber aesthetics to Pirate Island
Shattered Ice Coast.relations: Longstanding privateering rivalry with Pirate Island but significant shipwright exchange; close trade with Frost Marches.
Shattered Ice Coast.trade: Exports fish, ice, salvage and polar ship services; imports timber, food, metal and ceramics.
Shattered Ice Coast.historic_landmark: The Chain Beacons, a linked system of sea forts and rescue lights built after a catastrophic fleet loss.
Shattered Ice Coast.routes: Northern Beacon Route and the dangerous Outer Ice Passage toward Transit Isles.

The Crownlands.origin: Separate river and lowland towns gradually accepted common law around iron production, markets and defense, eventually forming the archipelago's strongest centralized state.
The Crownlands.identity: Civic order, public works, formal institutions and visible political hierarchy.
influences_given: planned plazas and civic arches across central regions
administrative models to Grand Exchange and Transit Isles
The Crownlands.relations: Friendly strategic rivalry with High Kingdom; uneasy dependence on Grand Exchange commerce; close food ties with Breadbasket and Hearthlands.
The Crownlands.trade: Exports iron-related goods, administration and security; imports food, timber, stone, luxury craft and maritime resources.
The Crownlands.historic_landmark: The Concord Gate, expanded after the Three Bridges War as both triumphal arch and treaty monument.
The Crownlands.routes: Royal Road to High Kingdom; Hearth Road to Hearthlands; Exchange Road to Grand Exchange.

The High Kingdom.origin: Mountain strongholds, monasteries and pass towns developed separately before unifying around control of high crossings and shared ceremonial traditions.
The High Kingdom.identity: Vertical monumentality, sacred landscapes, engineering prestige and fierce local autonomy beneath a shared crown.
influences_given: monastery and bridge-castle forms to neighboring highlands
prestige stonework to northern religious sites
The High Kingdom.relations: Historic rival of Crownlands but now a treaty partner; culturally close to Stone Highlands while regarding it as more utilitarian.
The High Kingdom.trade: Exports high-skill masonry, prestige craft and pass access; imports grain, timber, brewing goods and industrial components.
The High Kingdom.historic_landmark: The Three Bridges, monumental crossings rebuilt after the war that bears their name.
The High Kingdom.routes: Royal Road to Crownlands; Mason's Road to Stone Highlands; High Pilgrimage to mountain monasteries.

The Hearthlands.origin: Lake villages and inn-centered market communities grew around fisheries, orchards and sheltered crossings, forming a loose culture long before strong central government reached them.
The Hearthlands.identity: Hospitality, food, brewing, local festivals and settlement shaped around water and gathering places.
influences_received: Crownlands civic order in larger towns
influences_given: inn and covered-bridge traditions across travel routes
brewing culture throughout the central belt
The Hearthlands.relations: Generally trusted neutral neighbor; close to Breadbasket and Timberlands; provides social common ground between Crownlands and frontier cultures.
The Hearthlands.trade: Exports prepared food, brewing products and hospitality; imports bulk grain, timber, stone, ceramics and specialty ingredients.
The Hearthlands.historic_landmark: The Long Table Hall, a civic inn where several regional compacts were negotiated.
The Hearthlands.routes: Hearth Road linking Crownlands, Breadbasket and Timberlands; lake pilgrimage route to the abbey islands.

The Timberlands.origin: Independent forest clans and river mills gradually formed guilds to regulate cutting rights, replanting and dangerous long-distance log transport.
The Timberlands.identity: Master carpentry, stewardship, visible structural honesty and a belief that forests must remain larger than settlements.
influences_received: Breadbasket water-management law after the Greenbank Dispute
influences_given: timber framing to nearly every region
shipbuilding knowledge to Shattered Ice Coast and Pirate Island
The Timberlands.relations: Close but occasionally tense with Breadbasket over watersheds; strong craft ties to Hearthlands; commercially dependent on Grand Exchange.
The Timberlands.trade: Exports every wood and tree family plus finished timber goods; imports food, metal, stone and industrial components.
The Timberlands.historic_landmark: The Greenbank Grove, protected after the Greenbank Compact and never commercially harvested.
The Timberlands.routes: Log River to Grand Exchange; Greenbank Road to Breadbasket; carpenter routes into Hearthlands.

The Breadbasket.origin: Canal villages and farm estates formed cooperative water councils because irrigation, mills and flood control required decisions beyond a single settlement.
The Breadbasket.identity: Agricultural abundance, practical civic cooperation, seasonal markets and landscapes engineered for water and food.
influences_given: canal administration to Crownlands and Red Clay Basin
farm organization to Isles of Plenty
The Breadbasket.relations: Economically indispensable but politically modest; protective of water rights after the Greenbank Dispute.
The Breadbasket.trade: Exports bulk food, crops and bone-meal-supported agricultural goods; imports timber, stone, tools, ceramics and maritime specialties.
The Breadbasket.historic_landmark: The Seven Locks, canal works that became the symbol of the agricultural compact.
The Breadbasket.routes: Grain Canal to Grand Exchange; Hearth Road west; Greenbank routes north toward Timberlands.

The Grand Exchange.origin: Began as neutral seasonal docks used by several civilizations and became a permanent city because no single region could dominate the trade crossing without driving commerce elsewhere.
The Grand Exchange.identity: Negotiation, contracts, cosmopolitan neighborhoods, practical tolerance and relentless movement of goods.
influences_given: warehouse and customs models across ports
commercial law and guild organization across the archipelago
The Grand Exchange.relations: Necessary partner and recurring political rival of Crownlands; frequent conflict with Pirate Island over tariffs; deeply tied to Transit Isles.
The Grand Exchange.trade: Imports and re-exports nearly everything; specializes in storage, sorting, contracts, auctions and finance rather than primary production.
The Grand Exchange.historic_landmark: The Exchange Hall, built in layers by competing merchant guilds and intentionally containing materials from every major region.
The Grand Exchange.routes: All major trade circuits converge here; strongest links are Breadbasket grain canal, Timberlands log route and Transit freight lanes.

Engineer's Reach.origin: Formed when mechanics, redstone specialists, bridge crews and industrial investors created a permanent technical settlement outside older guild restrictions.
Engineer's Reach.identity: Experimentation, standardization, public demonstrations and pride in visible machinery.
influences_given: rail and automation systems to Transit Isles
industrial methods to Ember Coast and Grand Exchange
Engineer's Reach.relations: Commercially close to Grand Exchange; respectful rivalry with Stone Highlands engineers; dependent on Red Clay Basin materials while sometimes irritating Basin craftspeople with mass production.
Engineer's Reach.trade: Exports machinery, redstone systems and technical services; imports stone, brick, iron, wood, food and specialty components.
Engineer's Reach.historic_landmark: The Demonstration Viaduct, rebuilt repeatedly as new engineering techniques surpassed old ones.
Engineer's Reach.routes: Machine Road to Grand Exchange; industrial freight connection to Transit Isles; technical missions to Volcano and Ember Coast.

Artisan Coast.origin: Independent coastal workshops became a city when ceramicists, glaziers, dyers, builders and merchants chose proximity to shipping without accepting Grand Exchange guild control.
Artisan Coast.identity: Craft prestige, color, experimentation in surface and pattern, and neighborhood-scale production.
influences_given: decorative tile and glazing throughout wealthy districts
color traditions to Transit stations and Crownlands civic interiors
Artisan Coast.relations: Friendly craft rivalry with Red Clay Basin; commercially tied to Grand Exchange but culturally protective of workshop independence.
Artisan Coast.trade: Exports glass, concrete, colorworks, tile and decorative goods; imports sand-like raw materials, clay, dyes, fuel, timber and food.
Artisan Coast.historic_landmark: The Hundred Workshops, a connected sequence of courtyards where each generation alters the facades without replacing earlier work.
Artisan Coast.routes: Artisan Sea Road to Grand Exchange and Sapphire Coast; craft caravans toward Red Clay Basin.

The Haunted Marches.origin: Border hamlets repeatedly rebuilt after hostile-mob incursions and failed settlement waves. Over time survival practices became institutions and a distinctive martial-funerary culture.
The Haunted Marches.identity: Watchkeeping, guarded hospitality, memorial traditions and controlled use of dangerous resources.
influences_received: Hearthlands house forms hardened into fortified farmsteads
influences_given: defensive watch systems to nearby frontiers
mob-control expertise used by other regions
The Haunted Marches.relations: Defensive ally of Crownlands but distrustful of outside officials; culturally close to Blackfen herbalists and wary of overly romantic outsiders.
The Haunted Marches.trade: Exports hostile-mob drops, gunpowder, bones, arrows and string; imports food, light sources, timber, stone and brewing supplies.
The Haunted Marches.historic_landmark: The Unbroken Wall, expanded around older ruined settlements instead of replacing them.
The Haunted Marches.routes: Warden Road to Crownlands; Lantern Path to Blackfen shrines; guarded freight routes to Grand Exchange.

The Blackfen.origin: Wetland communities developed on piles and boardwalks because roads and heavy foundations were unreliable. Local navigation and herbal knowledge became more important than territorial boundaries.
The Blackfen.identity: Waterway memory, wetland stewardship, practical folklore, flexible settlement and decentralized authority.
influences_given: pile foundations to Sunken Coast rebuilding
herbal and wetland knowledge to Hearthlands and Haunted Marches
The Blackfen.relations: Old cultural kinship with Sunken Coast communities; frequent minor disputes over channels and salvage rights but strong mutual aid during floods.
The Blackfen.trade: Exports slime, swamp flora, potion-related goods, reeds and wetland craft; imports stone, grain, metal and dry storage goods.
The Blackfen.historic_landmark: The Lantern Boardwalk, a pilgrimage and navigation spine rebuilt as channels shift.
The Blackfen.routes: Reedway to Sunken Coast; Lantern Path toward Haunted Marches; ferry routes to Grand Exchange.

Stone Highlands.origin: Quarry settlements and pass villages formed around local stone knowledge long before neighboring monarchies sought their materials and engineers.
Stone Highlands.identity: Durability, structural honesty, guild mastery and suspicion of decorative excess unsupported by good construction.
influences_given: masonry and bridge engineering to Crownlands and High Kingdom
heavy construction knowledge to Volcano
Stone Highlands.relations: Culturally close to High Kingdom but proud of being older and more practical; technical rivalry with Engineer's Reach.
Stone Highlands.trade: Exports stone, geology products and skilled masons; imports food, timber, metal tools and decorative goods.
Stone Highlands.historic_landmark: The Neutral Bridge Yard, where the Three Bridges War peace terms were negotiated by master masons.
Stone Highlands.routes: Mason's Road to High Kingdom; quarry freight line to Grand Exchange; Stone-and-Fire route toward Volcano.

Red Clay Basin.origin: Dry mesa communities independently developed cisterns, courtyard settlements and high-temperature ceramics because water conservation and durable containers were essential.
Red Clay Basin.identity: Water wisdom, ceramics as both utility and art, shaded communal courts and strong craft lineages.
influences_given: brick to Engineer's Reach
terracotta and kiln craft to Artisan Coast and wealthy Crownlands districts
Red Clay Basin.relations: Proud craft rivalry with Artisan Coast; profitable but occasionally tense supplier relationship with Engineer's Reach.
Red Clay Basin.trade: Exports clay, brick, terracotta, ceramics and water-engineering expertise; imports timber, food, fuel, metal and marine goods.
Red Clay Basin.historic_landmark: The First Cistern Court, an ancient water complex still integrated into the capital's civic center.
Red Clay Basin.routes: Kiln Road to Artisan Coast; brick freight to Engineer's Reach; merchant route to Grand Exchange.

The Sunken Coast.origin: Older shore towns were transformed by the Drowning Years. Survivors rebuilt around tides, boats, seawalls and elevated storage rather than attempting to restore the old coastline.
The Sunken Coast.identity: Adaptation to changing water, fishing, salvage, tidal engineering and cultural memory of lost streets beneath the sea.
influences_given: tidal mills and flood gates to Blackfen and Sapphire Coast
salvage practices to Pirate Island
The Sunken Coast.relations: Strong mutual-aid tradition with Blackfen; friendly maritime competition with Sapphire Coast.
The Sunken Coast.trade: Exports fish, kelp, drowned/trident-related resources and tidal services; imports timber, grain, stone and manufactured tools.
The Sunken Coast.historic_landmark: The Drowned Bell Tower, preserved above submerged streets as a memorial and navigation mark.
The Sunken Coast.routes: Reedway to Blackfen; Blue Pilgrimage to Sapphire Coast; fishing routes toward Grand Exchange.

The Crystal Deep.origin: Modern communities formed around geodes, deep caves and ruins whose builders are unknown. Surface settlers gradually developed a distinct subterranean society shaped by sound, darkness and vertical access.
The Crystal Deep.identity: Research, controlled quiet, reverence for ancient geometry and a sharp distinction between temporary modern work and older ruins.
influences_given: acoustic and crystal aesthetics to religious architecture elsewhere
deep-exploration knowledge to Shrouded Isles expeditions
The Crystal Deep.relations: Cooperative with Stone Highlands researchers; secretive scholarly connection to Shrouded Isles that is only partly acknowledged publicly.
The Crystal Deep.trade: Exports amethyst, sculk, dripstone knowledge and rare cave resources; imports food, timber, metal and surface machinery.
The Crystal Deep.historic_landmark: The Silent Geometry, a monumental ruin older than all recorded regional histories.
The Crystal Deep.routes: Deep Lift to Transit freight lines; Resonance Pilgrimage through crystal monasteries; restricted expedition routes toward Shrouded Isles contacts.

The Volcano.origin: Communities formed around naturally accessible heat, basalt and lava, developing fortress-like foundries because ordinary timber settlement was impossible near the caldera.
The Volcano.identity: Forge prestige, heat discipline, heavy masonry and civic pride in dangerous industrial mastery.
influences_given: heat-resistant construction to Ember Coast
basalt monumental forms to several industrial regions
The Volcano.relations: Industrial elder and rival to Ember Coast; respects Stone Highlands builders; trades closely with Engineer's Reach while guarding forge traditions.
The Volcano.trade: Exports lava, basalt, heavy forge goods and heat-processing services; imports food, timber, specialty metal and technical components.
The Volcano.historic_landmark: The Caldera Forge, both civic hall and operating foundry.
The Volcano.routes: Stone-and-Fire Road to Stone Highlands; Ash Compact freight route to Ember Coast and Engineer's Reach.

Pirate Island.origin: Sailors, exiles, failed merchants, privateers and refugees from many regions accumulated in defensible coves where no neighboring state could easily impose law.
Pirate Island.identity: Personal allegiance, salvage, visible reuse, negotiated freedom and suspicion of centralized authority.
influences_given: improvised shipyard techniques
freeport culture and covert routes across maritime regions
Pirate Island.relations: Historic enemy and indispensable shadow partner of Grand Exchange; recurring naval rivalry with Sapphire Coast; mutual respect with Shattered Ice Coast shipwrights.
Pirate Island.trade: Imports almost everything through legal and illegal channels; exports ship repair, salvage, information, smuggling services and captured goods.
Pirate Island.historic_landmark: The Patchwork Citadel, built from captured stone, ship timbers and additions from many eras.
Pirate Island.routes: Freeport Circuit to Grand Exchange and Sapphire Coast; hidden smuggling routes through Transit and Sunken Coast waters.

The Ember Coast.origin: Mixed portal expeditions established fortified enclaves independently of older surface cities. Repeated failures forced settlers to develop a new culture organized around compartmentalization, guarded routes and dangerous specialized districts.
The Ember Coast.identity: Portal discipline, industrial fortification, controlled risk and pride in mastering hostile environments.
influences_received: Grand Exchange exchange practices in piglin/gold districts
influences_given: portal-fortress design to Transit long-distance hubs
Nether material aesthetics back into Volcano and Artisan Coast
The Ember Coast.relations: Competitive with Volcano over industrial prestige but bound by the Ash Compact; heavily dependent on surface food and logistics.
The Ember Coast.trade: Exports Nether-exclusive resources, gold/piglin goods, blaze/wither drops, froglights and Nether stone products; imports food, wood, water-dependent goods and surface machinery.
The Ember Coast.historic_landmark: The First Safe Court, the portal complex whose compartmentalized plan became the model for the region.
The Ember Coast.routes: Ash Compact route to Volcano and Engineer's Reach; guarded freight corridors into Transit Isles.

The Sapphire Coast.origin: Reef navigators and monument-adjacent settlements developed a marine civic culture in which underwater and shoreline spaces were treated as a single inhabited landscape.
The Sapphire Coast.identity: Navigation, formal marine architecture, reef stewardship and civic pride visible from the sea.
influences_given: sea-gate and lighthouse traditions
reef landscaping and water-arch motifs across southern ports
The Sapphire Coast.relations: Friendly competition with Sunken Coast; persistent anti-piracy rivalry with Pirate Island; strong merchant connection to Grand Exchange.
The Sapphire Coast.trade: Exports guardian/prismarine resources, coral-related goods, navigation services and marine craft; imports timber, food, ceramics and machinery.
The Sapphire Coast.historic_landmark: The Ceremonial Sea Gate, built after the Freeport Crisis as both defensive channel and civic monument.
The Sapphire Coast.routes: Blue Pilgrimage from Sunken Coast; merchant sea lane to Grand Exchange; southern route to Isles of Plenty.

The Isles of Plenty.origin: Tropical communities developed around year-round husbandry, orchards, bees and coastal exchange without the same need for dense fortification or heavy masonry found elsewhere.
The Isles of Plenty.identity: Open settlement, creature stewardship, shaded communal life, abundance and integration of farms with villages.
influences_given: tropical crop and husbandry practices to Hearthlands and Artisan Coast gardens
The Isles of Plenty.relations: Generally peaceful and commercially valuable; maintains close maritime ties with Sapphire Coast and resists overdevelopment by outside investors.
The Isles of Plenty.trade: Exports passive-creature goods, bamboo, melons, sugar cane, bees and tropical produce; imports stone, metal, machinery and northern specialties.
The Isles of Plenty.historic_landmark: The Open Market Grove, a civic center built around living trees rather than replacing them.
The Isles of Plenty.routes: Southern sea road to Sapphire Coast; produce lane toward Grand Exchange; passenger links through Transit Isles.

The Transit Isles.origin: Originally unrelated lighthouse, ferry and crossroads settlements. Common route problems gradually created a shared professional culture of pilots, innkeepers, engineers and station keepers.
The Transit Isles.identity: Movement, legibility, neutrality, standardized wayfinding and hospitality to strangers.
influences_given: common signage, emergency-harbor design and transfer standards used throughout the archipelago
The Transit Isles.relations: Formally neutral under the Transit Accords; politically courted by Crownlands and Grand Exchange because control of movement is strategically important.
The Transit Isles.trade: Exports transportation, rocket, ferry, repair and traveler services; imports nearly all raw materials and food.
The Transit Isles.historic_landmark: The Zero Marker, the route standard from which the modern interregional network is measured.
The Transit Isles.routes: Every major network crosses Transit territory; key systems include Grand Exchange freight, northern beacon routes, southern sea routes and long-distance flight paths.

The Shrouded Isles.origin: Younger than most regions. End explorers, researchers and settlers from several cultures established scattered enclaves, but long isolation and exposure to strange materials produced a society that no longer feels like any single parent culture.
The Shrouded Isles.identity: Secrecy, sparse settlement, controlled knowledge, unusual spatial proportions and a belief that some discoveries should remain hidden.
influences_received: mainland forms abstracted almost beyond recognition
influences_given: End materials and strange geometric ideas slowly appearing in elite mainland architecture
The Shrouded Isles.relations: Maintains discreet scholarly ties with Crystal Deep and necessary transport ties with Transit Isles; most other regions know little about its internal politics.
The Shrouded Isles.trade: Exports Enderman, shulker/storage, chorus/purpur, obsidian and special-system resources; imports food, ordinary wood, surface tools and supplies through controlled channels.
The Shrouded Isles.historic_landmark: The Veiled Observatory, whose proportions intentionally obscure where the original mainland design ends and End adaptation begins.
The Shrouded Isles.routes: Restricted Shroud Route through Transit Isles; secret scholarly exchange with Crystal Deep known as the Resonance Line.

cross_regional_routes.name: Northern Beacon Route
cross_regional_routes.purpose: winter travel, rescue, northern trade and pilgrimage

cross_regional_routes.name: Hearth Road
cross_regional_routes.purpose: central food, timber and civic exchange

cross_regional_routes.name: Grand Circuit
cross_regional_routes.purpose: high-volume freight, craft goods and technical exchange

cross_regional_routes.name: Mason's Road
cross_regional_routes.purpose: stone, builders, pilgrimage and historic military movement

cross_regional_routes.name: Reedway
cross_regional_routes.purpose: wetland exchange, herbal trade, salvage and guarded frontier travel

cross_regional_routes.name: Blue Pilgrimage
cross_regional_routes.purpose: maritime pilgrimage, fishing trade and southern passenger movement

cross_regional_routes.name: Stone-and-Fire Road
cross_regional_routes.purpose: heavy industry, masonry, portal engineering and technical freight

cross_regional_routes.name: Freeport Circuit
cross_regional_routes.purpose: legal trade, privateering history, ship repair and covert commerce

cross_regional_routes.name: Resonance Line
cross_regional_routes.purpose: restricted research traffic and long-distance expedition supply
